claims.text: Conventional tempered martensitic steel can exhibit a reproducible ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
A precise tempering schedule targeting a narrow embrittlement temperature window produces the transition.
The proposed transition is caused by impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Tempered martensitic steel in its as-tempered state is ductile at high temperatures.
Moderate-temperature holding provides sufficient atomic mobility for phosphorus or sulfur to segregate to grain boundaries.
Ductility is recovered after cooling to lower temperatures.
Segregated embrittling impurities reduce cohesion in grain-boundary regions.
Impurity segregation weakens grain-boundary bonding and causes a dramatic loss of ductility.
Above the embrittlement window, sufficient kinetic energy prevents impurity segregation and restores ductility.
Below the embrittlement window, insufficient atomic mobility limits impurity segregation and restores ductility.
The steel will be ductile at high temperatures, brittle within a narrow intermediate window, and ductile again upon further cooling.
Without a targeted tempering schedule, the steel presents temper embrittlement less controllably.
The proposed transition is expected only in conventional alloys such as tempered martensitic steels.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys should not exhibit this transition.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys resist impurity segregation by design.
The identity and concentration of embrittling impurities vary with steel composition and influence transition severity.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says tempering creates grain-boundary segregation that reduces cohesion, but it also says merely cooling the already treated material restores ductility because low mobility limits segregation. Low mobility during cooling does not itself remove segregation already produced, so the stated mediator does not coherently explain the claimed low-temperature recovery.
